_note: Anchors are written BEFORE any candidate is seen, so they cannot be shaped by one. Every competency is a behaviour observable in an answer. Replace the content for your roles; keep the shape.

competencies.name: Problem decomposition
competencies.definition: Breaks an ambiguous problem into tractable parts, states assumptions, and identifies what would need to be true for the approach to work.

anchors.label: Does not decompose
anchors.description: Jumps to a solution without restating the problem. Assumptions stay implicit. When the problem is underspecified, either guesses silently or stalls.

anchors.label: Partial
anchors.description: Identifies one or two sub-problems but misses a major one. States some assumptions when prompted, not spontaneously.

anchors.label: Solid
anchors.description: Breaks the problem into sensible parts and states assumptions unprompted. Asks at least one clarifying question before solving.

anchors.label: Strong
anchors.description: Decomposition is clean and the parts are independently testable. Names what would falsify the approach. Prioritises which part to attack first and says why.

anchors.label: Exceptional
anchors.description: Reframes the problem in a way that makes it materially simpler, and justifies the reframing against the original constraints.

competencies.name: Technical depth
competencies.definition: Understands the systems they have worked on below the API surface, including failure modes and trade-offs actually encountered.

anchors.label: Surface only
anchors.description: Describes what a system did but not how. Cannot explain a choice beyond 'that is what we used'.

anchors.label: Shallow
anchors.description: Explains mechanism for the parts they wrote, but not the boundaries. Trade-offs are recited rather than reasoned.

anchors.label: Solid
anchors.description: Explains mechanism and at least one trade-off they made, with the reason. Knows a real failure mode of their system.

anchors.label: Strong
anchors.description: Explains a failure they diagnosed, how they localised it, and what the fix cost. Can say what they would do differently.

anchors.label: Exceptional
anchors.description: Explains a non-obvious interaction between components and why it was hard to see. Quantifies the impact.

competencies.name: Judgement about code quality
competencies.definition: Distinguishes changes that reduce future cost from changes that only look tidier, and can say which they would skip under time pressure.

anchors.label: No basis
anchors.description: Quality is stated as rules without reasons, or dismissed entirely.

anchors.label: Rule-following
anchors.description: Cites conventions correctly but cannot say what problem each prevents.

anchors.label: Solid
anchors.description: Ties at least one practice to a concrete cost it avoided. Recognises that some quality work is not worth doing.

anchors.label: Strong
anchors.description: Gives an example of deliberately accepting debt, the reason, and how it was tracked or repaid.

anchors.label: Exceptional
anchors.description: Articulates how they decide, not just what they decided, and applies it to an unfamiliar example in the interview.

competencies.name: Collaboration under disagreement
competencies.definition: Handles technical disagreement in a way that reaches a decision and keeps the working relationship intact.

anchors.label: Avoids or escalates
anchors.description: Either did not raise the disagreement or went straight to a manager. Describes colleagues as the obstacle.

anchors.label: Positional
anchors.description: Restated their own position more forcefully. Resolution came from seniority or exhaustion rather than evidence.

anchors.label: Solid
anchors.description: Sought the other person's reasoning and can state it accurately. A decision was reached and they supported it.

anchors.label: Strong
anchors.description: Changed position on evidence at least once, or found a test that settled it. Names what they got wrong.

anchors.label: Exceptional
anchors.description: Converted the disagreement into a shared criterion the team reused afterwards.

competencies.name: Communicating to non-specialists
competencies.definition: Explains technical constraints to someone without the background, so they can make a decision.

anchors.label: Does not adapt
anchors.description: Same jargon regardless of audience. Answers the question they wanted rather than the one asked.

anchors.label: Simplifies inaccurately
anchors.description: Removes jargon but loses the constraint that mattered, leaving the listener with a wrong model.

anchors.label: Solid
anchors.description: Explains the constraint in the listener's terms and checks understanding.

anchors.label: Strong
anchors.description: Frames the constraint as options with costs, so a non-specialist can actually choose.

anchors.label: Exceptional
anchors.description: Surfaces the decision the listener did not know they had, and equips them to make it.

questions.text: Tell me about a system you worked on where the hardest part was not the code. What made it hard, and how did you approach it?
probes: What did you assume at the start that turned out to be wrong?
What would have had to be true for a simpler approach to work?
How did you decide what to tackle first?

questions.text: Describe a production failure you diagnosed. Take me through how you localised it.
probes: What did you rule out, and how?
What did the fix cost, and what did you trade away?
What would you do differently now?

questions.text: Tell me about a time you deliberately shipped something you knew was not the right long-term solution.
probes: How did you decide that was the right call?
How was it tracked afterwards? What actually happened to it?

questions.text: Tell me about a technical disagreement with a colleague where you did not get your way.
probes: What was their reasoning? State it as they would.
What happened after the decision was made?

questions.text: Explain a technical constraint you had to get a non-technical stakeholder to accept. How did you explain it?
probes: What did they think before the conversation?
What decision did they end up making?
